newsitem.title: CHINA: China sees growing army of surplus rural labourers.
newsitem.headline: China sees growing army of surplus rural labourers.

text.p: China's army of surplus rural labourers could grow to more than 140 million people by the end of 2000, as farmers leave their land and officials struggle to arrange new jobs, the Xinhua news agency said on Friday.
The rural employment situation was far from optimistic, it quoted vice-minister of labour Lin Yongsan as telling a national conference in Beijing.
"If no effective measures are taken, the size of surplus rural labour could go beyond 140 million by the end of 2000, even larger than its present size," Lin said.

Over the next five years a huge imbalance would continue to exist between the supply and demand for rural labour, and finding work for people from the countryside would remain a major problem, the official agency quoted him as saying.
The government was not expected to be able to create more than 70 million jobs for the 210 million rural workers seeking employment during the next five years, he said.
Around 130 million rural workers were already counted as surplus labour, Xinhua said.
Decreasing arable land area, a lack of funds and surging agricultural production costs had dampened farmers' enthusiasm and led to a rise in surplus labour, Lin said.
China's vigorous township industries, which have long absorbed large numbers of rural labourers, now faced problems that limited their ability to take on workers, he said.

"It is also unrealistic to expect cities and towns, which are poor in infrastructure and have been already heavily burdened by the large number of laid-off workers from state enterprises, to contribute much to rural employment," he said.

To create more job opportunities, China could boost agricultural inputs and deepen reforms of township enterprises, while also making use of the unexploited natural resources and trying to develop new sectors and businesses, he said.
The reasonable flow of rural labour should be aided by a breaking down of the administrative controls that barred rural residents from moving to urban areas, he said.
"Some counties or cities should lead...in abolishing the distinctions between city and countryside, and setting up an employment system that is based upon fair competition and free choice," he said.
